summary: Describes version 2 of the Session Announcement Protocol, a multicast session directory announcement protocol, along with security and scalability issues for implementors. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: This is a way to announce on a network that a live event is starting and how to join.

subtitle: How multicast session directories announce live sessions, with a fixed port, a header, and an announcement rate cap.

tldr.problem: People who want to join a multicast conference or broadcast need a way to learn that it exists and how to join, without a central server to ask.
tldr.mechanism: An announcer periodically multicasts a packet containing a session description (normally SDP) to a well-known address and port, with the same scope as the session. Listeners collect these announcements, and an optional authentication header protects changes and deletions.
tldr.outcome: SAP is an Experimental protocol for announcing long-lived wide-area multicast sessions. It is not timely and adds no reliability beyond best-effort UDP.

today: RFC 2974 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes version 2 of SAP.

sections.title: What SAP Does
sections.content:
The Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) describes how a multicast session is announced so that others can participate. A SAP announcer periodically multicasts an announcement packet to a well-known multicast address and port. A SAP listener learns which multicast scopes it is in, listens on the well-known address and port for those scopes, and over time learns of all announced sessions.

There is no rendezvous mechanism: the announcer does not know whether any listeners exist, and no reliability is added to standard best-effort UDP/IP. The announcement carries a session description, which SHOULD be accompanied by an authentication header. Sessions are described with the Session Description Protocol (SDP), defined in a companion memo.
sections.eli5: The crier shouts the news on a schedule and does not check who is listening. Anyone nearby who hears it can find out about the show.

sections.title: Addresses, Port and Scope
sections.content:
An announcement is multicast with the same scope as the session it announces, which keeps local announcements local. SAP announcements MUST be sent on port 9875 and SHOULD use an IP time-to-live of 255.

  • IPv4 global scope: sessions use addresses 224.2.128.0 to 224.2.255.255 and announcements go to 224.2.127.254.
  • IPv4 administrative scope: announcements go to the highest multicast address in the relevant scope zone.
  • IPv6: announcements go to FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFE, where X is the 4-bit scope value.

Several announcers may announce one session for robustness, as long as the announcements are identical and the combined rate equals what a single announcer would use. Multiple announcements must be signed with the same key or listeners treat them as separate.
sections.eli5: The announcement goes to a special shared mailbox for each area, so a small local event is only announced locally and not across the world.

sections.title: Timing, Deletion and Modification
sections.content:
Announcers share a bandwidth limit that, if not otherwise specified, SHOULD be assumed to be 4000 bits per second for all announcements on one SAP group. The base interval is max(300; (8*no_of_ads*ad_size)/limit) seconds, and a random offset is added so announcements do not synchronize. Each announcer recalculates before sending, which prevents bursts at startup and when a network partition heals.

A session can be removed three ways. Explicit timeout: the description holds an end-time that has passed. Implicit timeout: nothing heard for ten times the announcement period, or one hour, whichever is greater. Explicit deletion: a deletion packet arrives, which SHOULD carry a valid authentication header matching earlier announcements.

To modify a session, the announcer simply announces the new description with a changed message identifier hash. A modified announcement must be signed by the same key as the cached one, or, if the cached one was unauthenticated, come from the same host. Otherwise it is treated as a new, separate announcement.
sections.eli5: The crier repeats the news every so often, but more people shouting means each one waits longer. If the news stops for a long time, listeners forget the show.

sections.title: The SAP Packet
sections.content:
The SAP header starts with these fields: version V (MUST be 1), an address type bit A (0 for IPv4, 1 for IPv6), a reserved bit R, a message type bit T (0 announcement, 1 deletion), an encryption bit E, a compressed bit C (zlib), an 8-bit authentication length counted in 32-bit words, and a 16-bit message identifier hash. These are followed by the originating source (32 or 128 bits), optional authentication data, an optional payload type, and the payload.

The message identifier hash and originating source together identify the version of an announcement. Announcers SHOULD NOT set either to zero, a practice from the older SAPv0. The payload type is a MIME type string ended by a zero byte, and all implementations MUST support application/sdp. Other types are NOT RECOMMENDED, since there is no negotiation. Packets SHOULD stay under 1 kilobyte to avoid fragmentation.
sections.eli5: Each announcement has a small label on the front saying who sent it, which version it is, and whether it is a new announcement or a cancellation.

sections.title: Encryption, Authentication and Attacks
sections.content:
Encryption is NOT RECOMMENDED on groups with many receivers who cannot decrypt, because it wastes their bandwidth. The RFC provides the E bit but does not specify an algorithm or key distribution.

The authentication header holds a digital signature over the whole packet and is not tied to one mechanism. Type 0 is PGP format, type 1 is CMS format, and other values SHOULD be ignored. It lets receivers verify that changes and deletions are permitted, and sometimes identify the creator if a trusted certificate is available. The rules for modification stop a malicious user from adding an authentication header to an announcement and then deleting it, and stop a spoofed announcement from blocking the original.

The RFC describes a denial of service by flooding with low-TTL announcements for high-TTL sessions, which could drop a legitimate announcement rate below a tenth of the expected rate at remote sites. It offers no mechanism against it.
sections.eli5: A signature lets listeners know that a change or cancellation really came from whoever announced the show, so a prankster cannot cancel it.

sections.title: Scalability and Proxy Caches
sections.content:
SAP is meant for long-lived wide-area multicast sessions. It is not especially timely: announcements repeat on the order of tens of minutes, so a new listener waits a long time to hear the full set.

To reduce this delay, the RFC recommends proxy caches. A proxy listens to all SAP groups in its scope and keeps a list of sessions with the time each was last heard. A starting listener can download that list from the local proxy. The protocol for contacting the proxy is not specified.
sections.eli5: If you walk into town and the crier only repeats every so often, you could wait a long time. A helper who writes down every announcement can tell you the list right away.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Address type: 0 is IPv4, 1 is IPv6.

fields.name: Auth Len
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words of authentication data.

fields.name: Msg ID Hash
fields.desc: With the originating source, identifies this version of the announcement.
